walkthroughs.body_html:
Area of Study 1: Instrumental Music 1700-1820 — a core area of GCSE Music.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Area of Study 1: Instrumental Music 1700-1820 brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Area of Study 1: Instrumental Music 1700-1820.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: Which three solo instruments feature in Bach's Brandenburg Concerto No. 5?
options: Flute, violin and harpsichord
Oboe, horn and organ
Two trumpets and timpani
Cello, viola and lute

mcqs.q: Beethoven's 'Pathetique' Sonata is in which key?
options: C minor
C major
G major
E flat minor

mcqs.q: In a concerto grosso, the concertino is what?
options: The small group of soloists
The full string ensemble
The slow middle movement
The final cadence

mcqs.q: What is the role of the basso continuo?
options: To provide the bass line with improvised chords above it
To play the main melody
To conduct the ensemble
To double the flute part

mcqs.q: Does Brandenburg Concerto No. 5 feature a piano solo?
options: No - the keyboard soloist plays the harpsichord, the standard keyboard instrument of Bach's time.
The brilliant keyboard part in Brandenburg No. 5 is written for piano.
The only difference is that Classical pieces are always louder.
The keyboard part is played on a church organ with pedals.

mcqs.q: Does the slow Grave introduction of the 'Pathetique' disappear after the opening?
options: The introduction is heard once and never comes back.
The keyboard part is played on a church organ with pedals.
No - its material returns during the movement, dramatically interrupting the fast music.
The Grave is repeated unchanged at the start of every bar.

mcqs.q: Are Baroque and Classical just two names for the same style?
options: Music from 1700 and music from 1800 sound essentially identical.
The keyboard part is played on a church organ with pedals.
The only difference is that Classical pieces are always louder.
No - Baroque music features continuo, ornamented lines and terraced dynamics, while Classical style prefers balanced phrases, clearer textures and graded dynamics.
